source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The elevation can support a prerenal process related to water depletion or reduced renal perfusion when interpreted with the clinical picture.","B":"The elevation specifically proves postrenal urinary obstruction regardless of the client's volume status or other findings.","C":"The elevation demonstrates improved glomerular filtration because BUN rises when renal clearance becomes more efficient.","D":"The elevation is unrelated to hydration or renal perfusion and should not influence assessment of a volume-depleted client."}}
source_row.rationale: BUN can increase in prerenal states such as water depletion and reduced renal perfusion. Option A appropriately interprets the result in the clinical context without treating BUN as diagnostic by itself. B overstates specificity, C reverses the meaning, and D is false.
source_row.source_detail: Clinical Information/Interpretation: BUN may rise in prerenal states including water depletion and reduced renal perfusion/cardiac decompensation; BUN and creatinine are interpreted together with the clinical picture and other data. Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories BUN test catalog entry 81793; live-rechecked 2026-08-15. source_row.stem: A client with vomiting and poor intake is clinically volume depleted and has an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Which interpretation is most appropriate?
